Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system works on networking and knowing people, including the publication system. The fact that the student has to obtain a recommendation from the supervisor for any post-doctoral position is an example feature of a system that is stuck in the old era. And the student is extremely lucky if the supervisor is friendly, knowledgeable and most importantly, has the welfare of the student and their career as one of his/her priorities. I was unlucky. But, in my opinion, it is the fault of the system to have such a highly skewed power structure. The student is guaranteed to be exploited, by design.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

Q26.text: The academic system is, to put it charitably, a structure designed for a different era. The emphasis on publications over impact, credentialing over contribution, strikes me as legacy architecture — functional in places, genuinely broken in others. Coming in from outside, I can see both intellectual richness that justifies the whole enterprise and systemic incentives that would puzzle any reasonable outside observer. Reform feels overdue, though I'm not sure the institution knows it yet.

Q16.text: The question of whether my research will actually reach its intended audience — community organizations rather than other academics — concerns me more than anything methodological. there's also the quieter impostor-syndrome question: whether late entry into the academy earns the same intellectual standing, or whether one's contributions are always read through lens of novelty rather than substance.

Q55.text: That the institution's relationship with community-facing research is more ambivalent than I expected. Journals want theory; communities want tools. Knowing that gap existed from day one would have sharpened my design considerably — I'd have built the translation work in from the start rather than retrofitting it now, which is honestly a harder problem than any methodological one I've faced.

Q41.text: Pro bono research, likely affiliated with an NGO or university in a non-salaried capacity. I'm past the stage where career advancement drives the work.

Q60.text: Only that surveys like this one matter more than they're typically credited for — aggregate experience, honestly reported, is how institutions learn anything at all. I hope the data is actually used.

Q17.text: The permission to think slowly. Outside the academy, sustained inquiry without an immediate deliverable is a luxury most careers don't allow — here, it's the job. And honestly, at this stage of life, that's not a minor thing.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: As a late career-changer, I have seen the institutional attitude shift from "sink or swim" indifference to a genuine concern with student success. While this is undoubtedly enlightened self-interest on the part of the academy, it is a good first step. The next challenge is preparing grads for real careers. I notice that the concern with the endless postdoc cycle is gaining traction. A societal change, where science is seen not only as credible, but essential to our survival in every sphere, would help create the right atmosphere for bright new minds to flourish and contribute. Here in the USA, this is a problem at present.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Create a plan early, and refine it as often as necessary. A flawed or incomplete plan is better than no plan at all. Think of your coursework not as an externally-imposed checklist, but as a set of building-blocks for the finished product. Make every course count for something you plan to use. Take the opportunity to tailor electives and directed study coursework to your individual plan.

Q26.text: A well-veiled pyramid scheme, honestly -- graduate students are inexpensive labor generating grants and publications while PIs accumulate credit and external funding. The incentive structure doesn't reward good mentorship; it rewards output, and those two things are rarely aligned. I went in idealistic and came out clear-eyed about what the system actually values, which isn't the people inside it.

Q16.text: The way my PI handles personal leave -- or rather, refuses to -- has been genuinely demoralizing. I missed a family event because I was made to feel the lab couldn't function without me for two days. And comments I've heard about maternity leave make it pretty clear that having a life outside the PhD is viewed as a professional liability, not a right.

Q17.text: The research itself, when it's actually working — the moment a result coheres or an argument clicks into place. That part is genuinely satisfying. It's just increasingly hard to access that feeling when the surrounding structure is designed to extract rather than support you.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's becoming clear to me that the academic system constitutes a well-veiled pyramid scheme.  PIs think that grad school is the same as it was for them, and treat their students accordingly.  This is surprising to me, considering success as a scientist requires one to keep up with changing information.  For some reason, there's a blind spot where grad students are concerned.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: My PhD program advertised 4 weeks of time off per year, and a generous maternal leave policy.  The promise of a work-life balance lured me it, but my PI does not allow this much time off, and I often end up working through the weekend.  I can't even take two days off to attend an out-of-state funeral without there being unpleasant consequences.  This results in even lower total work output, because I'm tired and depressed all the time and more likely to make mistakes.  My PI has also remarked to at least one student that not electing to come back from maternity leave early means you don't care enough about science to be successful.

Q26.text: Experience in academia depends greatly on the department, environment, and university one is attending. Q26.text: Slow!!! So many hierarchical layers to go through before being able to make any meaningful change to the system. Having worked both in industry and academia, I also think academia is as money-driven as industry. The only difference being where the money is coming from. PhD students (UK) are also kept under a regime that makes them students, hence unable to unionise, while getting many hours out of them for a stipend that is frankly insufficient compared to our level of expertise. Also, the higher up you go, the more male and white-dominated the environment becomes. Q26.text:
Exploitative by design. You come in idealistic, grateful even, and slowly realise the whole system runs on cheap labour dressed up as "training." Low pay, no security, no transferable skills, publications that go nowhere. and the support structure is basically decorative.

What gets me is it's not accidental -- the incentives are set up so institutions extract value and hand you a credential that may or may not mean anything. I've put in 8 years. I'm not sure I'd call that an education.

Q16.text:
Family separation, honestly. My partner is overseas, I missed a funeral back home because leaving risked the visa. You just can't -- the risk is too high, so you grieve from a distance and then go back to the bench.

And the trap of it. Visa status means quitting isn't really an option even when everything in you says it should be. nobody talks about that openly. The formal wellbeing stuff doesn't touch any of it.

Q55.text: That it's not a meritocracy. Working hard and being good at the science doesn't translate to anything reliable -- jobs, pay, stability. I was a shit scientist who got better but the system doesn't care about that arc. it just needs bodies at the bench.

Q41.text: Anything that gets me out of academia, tbh. Industry, NGO, I don't care -- just something with a salary and job security that doesn't depend on my supervisor's grant renewal.

Q60.text:
Honestly, just that the wellbeing surveys and the mental health resources and all the "we care about our PhD students" messaging -- none of it addresses the structural stuff. Visa traps, poverty wages, geographic isolation from family. You can't therapy your way out of a system designed like this.

I hope someone actually reads these and it changes something. I doubt it, but I hope.

Q17.text: The autonomy, I guess. Nobody tells me exactly when to show up or leave. that's about it honestly. Everything else has been ground down.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I studied for over 8 years to be where I am now. I do not have student debt. I was a straight As student in school and in college. But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I cannot network or promote myself. I do not write well. If I graduate without a paper, I am looking at a mediocre lab postdoc position at best with median year salary ~$45k. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

I will never be in the same country that my family is in because my expertise is not valued there at all (and not valued here so much but I can buy food). Two of my close relatives died and I did not come to say my good byes. My boyfriend is doing PhD in a different country. I hate this.

Q26.text: There are no incentives for professors to be excellent mentors. This is not because of any individual professor, but is a systemic issue. Government grants are not awarded based on a professor's ability to mentor. Grants are only awarded based on the professor's ability to carry out research. Universities hire professors based on their likeability, ability to carry out research, ability to acquire research funding, and ability to market their research in the form of publications, talks, and acclaim.

Q60.text: I think the relationship between industry and academia is perverse. Industry profits from public investment in academic research, and has no obligations to provide any societal benefit with those profits. National or non-profit labs should take academic research to the public. Public investment, public profits, societal benefits. The pharmaceutical industry is an exemplar of this relationship. Every drug has relied on public funding, yet no publicly funded patent returns those investments back into scientific grants. This change occurred during Reagan administration when patents became university rather than government grant office property.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q26.text: Honestly, it feels like a system that was designed for people who dont have to worry about money, and then kind of just... kept going without ever questioning that assumption. The mentorship structures are inconsistent at best, and there's no real accountability when things go wrong -- you're mostly left to figure it out on your own while the institution collects your cheap labour and moves on. I still care about the research but I've stopped pretending that caring is enough to build a life on.

Q16.text: The mental health side of it, honestly -- I came in already carrying debt that wasnt going anywhere, and the stipend barely covers rent, let alone absorbs the baseline financial stress. I dont think I understood how much that would compound over time, or how little the institution would actually care once you're in.

Q55.text: That the stipend is not a temporary inconvenience you push through -- its a structural feature of a system that has decided your time and financial wellbeing are acceptable costs, and that feeling doesnt really get better as you advance. I wish someone had been honest with me about that before I signed anything, because I think I would have made very different decisions about whether to take on more debt to be here.

Q41.text: Industry. Something with a real salary and actual work-life balance.

Q60.text: Just that I hope someone actually reads these responses and doesnt treat them as data points to aggregate into nothing. There are real structural problems here -- financial, mentorship, accountability -- and they're not going to get fixed by adding another wellness workshop. I'm probably leaving academia when I finish and I dont think that's a personal failure, I think it's a rational response to a system that doesn't actually support the people in it.

Q17.text: The research itself, when I actually get to do it. That part still holds my interest -- the questions are genuinely interesting and I like having the space to follow an idea somewhere without someone asking if it's commercially viable. But its a smaller and smaller fraction of the actual experience, and honestly its getting harder to enjoy in isolation from everything else around it.

Q26.text: Good things: intellectual freedom. Bad: Glorifying over working, low stipend, competing for grants is stressful, lack of work boundaries on weekends/during holidays, too much emphasis on applied and not basic research. If I could change one thing about academia, it would be to make universities do 70% basic and 30% applied research. The university is starting to look too much like industry- just let grad students do basic research and stop emphasizing man made metrics of success like impact factors and opportunities for application. The best applications often seem to come as by-products of people doing basic research (PCR, CRISPR, etc.). Stop making scientists grovel about their impact, just let them study nature.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: Peer review needs to be more rigorous; initial screening for falsified data, re-used images, etc. The quality of our peer review determines the quality of our science and collective understanding. We need to revamp this- I am worried about how many poorly designed studies and misinterpretation of results are published, and how it is clouding our body of knowledge and leading us down fields and research paths that just aren't real or true. We need a generation that is more discerning and doesn't just trust something because it is published; in that sense, I'm worried about the state and fate of science.

Q26.text: Structurally underfunded and dependent on informal networks that not everyone can access. There are genuine intellectual communities worth being part of, but the institutional scaffolding -- career support, timeline realism, pastoral care -- seems designed for a different era. I came in optimistic and I'm still not bitter exactly, but I'm a lot clearer-eyed about what the system actually delivers versus what it promises.

Q16.text: The political environment around public sector hiring is something that weighs on me -- I'd prefer government work but hiring freezes and budget cycles make that feel increasingly speculative rn. Also, being the first student through this program means there's no one to ask "is this normal?" which is its own kind of low-grade stress.

Q55.text: That the timeline is essentially a fiction. Not always a deliberate one -- supervisors and departments often believe their own optimism -- but the four-year PhD is a normative aspiration more than a realistic plan, and nobody says that clearly at the start. Knowing it earlier would have changed how I set expectations and, honestly, how much I blamed myself when things took longer than advertised.

Q41.text: Government policy or public sector work, though that feels increasingly uncertain given current hiring conditions. Consulting or academia are also on the table if that doesn't pan out.

Q17.text: The intellectual community, honestly. Being around people who think carefully about hard problems and actually want to argue about methodology -- that part's been worth it. I don't take it for granted the way I might have at the start.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: There isn't a lot of sympathy for students going through the process. Advisers and mentors have the mindset of "well I did it, so you should be able to do it too" in regards to work-life balance, low income, and general stress levels. They don't consider what going through the system has done to them or whether it impacted them negatively. In addition, many advisers have chosen to enter academia; therefore, their career advice is generally targeted to that area.

Q26.text:
Broken in ways that aren't random — they're structural. The incentives reward publication volume over mentorship, grant acquisition over genuine training. My PI is brilliant but essentially absent, and I've come to realize that's not unusual, it's the norm. The whole system treats PhD students as cheap labor with a credential stapled on.

Honestly, I love the intellectual environment and I'd fight to preserve universities as institutions — but the graduate training model specifically needs to be rebuilt from scratch. Stipends that haven't kept pace with housing costs, no real career development infrastructure, supervisors with zero accountability for student outcomes. it's designed for a world that no longer exists, and people are paying for that mismatch with years of their lives.

Q16.text:
The debt situation honestly keeps me up at night. I took on loans expecting an academic job market that basically doesn't exist anymore, and my stipend has never come close to covering living expenses in this city. I'm at a stage where I should be thinking about buying a house, starting a family — and instead I'm doing the math on whether a postdoc would just defer insolvency by two years.

Also the mental health piece. I've watched multiple cohort-mates leave or take medical leave, and the institutional response is always "here's a hotline." it's not a counseling access problem, it's a structural one.

Q55.text: How non-linear the exit ramps are. I came in thinking the path was obvious — dissertation, postdoc, faculty position — and it took me three years to realize that path is essentially closed for most people, and the skills I was building had real value OUTSIDE academia. I wish someone had told me that on day one instead of letting me plan around a fiction.

Q41.text: Consulting or policy. Somewhere my analytical skills actually compound into something financially stable.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this data actually gets used. Too many surveys like this get buried in a report nobody reads. The problems are documented to death — what's missing is institutional will to fix them, and I'm not holding my breath.

Q17.text: The intellectual environment, genuinely. Being surrounded by people who care deeply about hard problems -- that part I'll actually miss. Everything else, not so much.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Broken. The wages are skewed. The incentives for faculty to publish in high impact factor journals make graduate students not have as many publications. There's fierce competition for grants which incentivizes cheating. The goal for the graduate student is to graduate and find employment but the goal for the faculty is to produce research and papers, thus these are at conflict. As a grad student becomes well trained, the faculty don't want to let them graduate because they have cheap, well trained, labor. Academic postdoc positions are the same. They're lowly paid but highly competent individuals. Faculty in universities still aren't aware of the data regarding competition for new faculty positions (despite serving on search panels). The whole system is broken.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The biggest, most overwhelming concern for the entirety of my PhD is trying to find good employment afterwards that can cover my student debt and allow me to start a family. Unfortunately, academic postdoc positions in the US do not pay enough to do this, which means I have to find a non-default path.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Good science and good management/leadership do not overlap. My PI is a great scientist but he is a TERRIBLE manager. This is likely why the average time to degree for my lab is 8 years when the department average is 6.5. He's incredibly hands off, provides no positive feedback, and discourages many things. You have to fight tooth and nail to get what you want unless you're his favorite student.

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: One that intersects with the life sciences but doesn't require bench research. I'd be happy continuing computational (genomic) research. I enjoy meetings and administrative/leadership/management work. Perhaps a policy analyst and strategy position. I'm currently targeting management consulting, executive recruiting, and policy analyst positions for application.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: We don't have an excess of people with PhD degrees. The world needs more highly educated people. We have a broken system that provides incentive for poor quality of life for graduate students and postdocs -- low pay, aggressive competition, long hours, discouragement from leaving the academic environment. This can be fixed, but it needs to be a top-down move away from the publish or perish environment. Even more faculty positions aren't necessary. Staff research positions would be great. Tenure-track teaching positions (divide the labor so some faculty are almost full time research, many are teaching) would make a significant difference. Put hard caps on graduate programs (6 years) to force program progression. Many people in my program don't defend their prospectus until year 5 which is COMPLETELY inappropriate. There is no department or university recourse for this.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: There are far more opportunities available for postgraduate students in the USA/EU, many of my friends and colleagues in the field who did their Masters degree abroad easily found PhD positions at top ranking institutions despite having no publications in the field (or often any publications at all) and mediocre grades. As a department we also regularly experience what we perceive as discrimination from reviewers towards third world universities, even when the results are objectively valuable and can be quickly reproduced with no effort (such as running a script with fully free and open source code). Many reviewers force us to cite their own papers in the manuscript before accepting our publication (despite being anonymous it is obvious when the authorship fields of these papers all contain the same researcher). Often the work is not significant or the results are less competative than other papers already cited in the manuscript.  In short it is very difficult (but certainly possible) to get in to the right networks for your career if you're coming from the wrong institution. The quality of your research is largely irrelevant, even in fields where problems have objective and established metrics for the quality of solutions.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The lack of respect for my job as a PhD student from the academy, some of my peers and society in general. My PhD is a job, I work full time on it and however I am only payed 50% (in Germany) of my salary because I am "student". When I complain that this is unfair, that I am not being payed for my full work hours or my extra hours (that are always expected of me as a PhD student); I am told that 1) I should be grateful for even getting paid, other disciplines are not 2) I benefit from student discounts so I should not complain for receiving less (I would happily give away my student discounts if I was payed a full salary!) 3) I should be happy because I am doing my passion job (passion is not going to feed me in my retirement). Not being entitle to a full salary, extra hours or even a contract that will allow us to receive some help after our working years is destroying our future before it even starts.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I did not start my PhD directly after the masters, I was working sometime as a research assistant. So by the time I decided to do a PhD I knew exactly why I was doing it and what were some of the possible challenges. As such I was prepared to keep going despite having to change my first PI (due to PI sickness) and restarting my PhD after 2 years and despite having a new PI now that is not meeting my expectations. So, I do think i was prepared to do a PhD when I started. Personally, from what I see around me, I would just tell everyone to not do a PhD right after the master/bachelor but to take their time and to find if a PhD is really what they want to do.

Q26.text: It's a system that genuinely rewards intellectual curiosity and long-term thinking, which I value, but the machinery around that — the funding allocation, the lab politics, the administrative processes that seem designed to obscure rather than facilitate — makes it incredibly difficult for mature-age students without a pre-existing network to actually get the resources they need to do the work. And honestly the opacity is the most corrosive part; you can adapt to scarcity if you understand the rules, but when the rules themselves are unarticulated and seem to shift depending on who you know, that's when it becomes demoralising.

Q16.text: The mental load of starting over professionally at this stage is something I genuinely underestimated -- the isolation that comes from not already belonging to a lab community, and honestly the sense that every administrative delay costs me more than it would someone earlier in their career. Time isn't neutral when you've already had one professional life.

Q55.text: That lab placement is essentially a social negotiation, not an administrative process, and no amount of prior professional experience equips you for the reality that your first-year trajectory depends almost entirely on informal relationships that pre-exist your arrival -- relationships you have no way to cultivate before you're already embedded in a system that's largely moved on without you. I came in thinking merit and preparation would translate, and they do, up to a point, but the invisible architecture of who sponsors whom and which lab has tacit priority for resources is just not documented anywhere, and honestly no one's going to tell you until you've already made the wrong assumptions.

Q41.text: Neuroscience research, ideally with a translational focus that draws on my background in microbiology and statistics.

Q60.text: The funding situation has been the single most disorienting part of this process, and I say that as someone who's navigated genuinely complex professional environments before -- I just wasn't prepared for how much of the actual research capacity here depends on informal understandings that aren't visible until you're already on the wrong side of them. I do want to say that the intellectual work itself remains genuinely compelling, and I haven't lost sight of why I came back to do this. But the structural dysfunction -- the lab overcrowding, the way resource decisions get made without any traceable rationale -- that's the thing I'd want whoever reads this to actually sit with, because it isn't incidental, its load-bearing for whether students like me can do what we came to do.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. Getting to pursue questions that actually matter to me after 25 years of working within other people's frameworks -- that part has been worth it.

I am now trying to do the same research under neuroscience and link into different labs as I design an experiment. The benefit is I am not tied to any one lab but it increases the stress around the experimental stages of my degree due to not gaining access to a lab or failing to get funding. I was very disappointed by the faculty allowing students to be enrolled part time but work full time as this also was not reflected in lab availability as well as very costly in lab equipment and consumables being used at a full time rate rather than a part time rate which drained the lab budget causing the lab to almost run out of money and engage in talks of letting go of the post docs because of funding issues around ability to pay them.

Q26.text: The academic system has genuine strengths -- intellectual rigor, collaborative potential, meaningful work -- but structural accountability gaps are real. Supervisors with clinical commitments often lack bandwidth to mentor adequately, and there are few formal mechanisms to address this. Q16.text: The lack of structured support for students experiencing supervisory difficulties has been a concern -- there's no clear escalation pathway short of formal complaints, which most students are understandably reluctant to pursue. career development resources also feel underdeveloped for those interested in non-academic trajectories.

Q55.text: How little formal protection exists for students in problematic supervisory arrangements. Q60.text: I would like to add a common issue that graduate students in biomedical research within my department face whenever they are supervised by medical doctors, which is lack of accessibility. Due to the demanding schedule medical doctors usually have, it is not easy for them to balance between their clinical and research duties. Personally, I found that the clinical and administrative responsibilities are almost always prioritized over supervisory duties. Sometimes, two months or more pass before I have face-time with my supervisor, and I end up seeking help from other principal investigators. I wish the department was more flexible regarding appointing co-advisors in case the principal advisor fails to demonstrate commitment to mentoring their trainees.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's pretty exploitative — the whole structure seems designed to extract cheap labour from students in exchange for a credential that's becoming less valuable by the year. Advisors benefit from having motivated, inexpensive researchers, and there's almost no accountability when that relationship curdles. I dont think it's accidental; the system works exactly as intended for the people at the top of it.

Q16.text: The mental health aspect, honestly — there's this ambient dread that I don't think gets taken seriously enough institutionally. And the financial reality of it: I'm doing skilled work for stipend pay while watching peers in industry pull in three times as much. it's hard not to do that math every few months and feel like I made a mistake.

Q55.text: How much the supervisor relationship determines everything. I treated choosing an advisor like choosing a collaborator; I should have treated it like choosing someone who controls your professional survival for five years. The power asymmetry is absolute in a way no one tells you upfront, and by the time you fully understand it, you're already in it.

Q60.text: The system largely runs on the assumption that PhD students are too invested to complain loudly, and that's probably true — by the time you realize how the game works, you've sunk years into it. Q17.text: The intellectual problems, when I actually get to work on them. That part's genuinely good.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I have a very dismal view of the academic system in general. The majority of my work has almost nothing to do with "education" and instead is truly work being done for my professor that has very little chance of benefiting me or advancing my career independently. In the resource constrained environment of University research, I understand the structural advantage of using a large army of underpaid/overworked graduate students to slog through the work, but the system seems to avoid any sense of good management or efficient work/support. The majority of my time is wasted, but because my time is so inexpensive, this is viewed as acceptable.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

There's real intellectual richness here, and I don't want to dismiss that, but the gap between what institutions say about student wellbeing and what they actually do about it is... pretty wide, in my experience. it doesn't make me want to leave academia exactly, but it does make me think hard about what other paths might look like.

Q55.text: That the department's interest in your wellbeing is mostly procedural. I came in thinking there'd be more genuine mentorship, more people checking in because they cared — and there is some of that, honestly, but it's not the default. you kind of have to build that for yourself, which is fine, I've managed, but it would've been useful to know going in rather than realizing it halfway through year two.

Q41.text: Science communication, maybe government or industry. Still figuring it out honestly.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually gets used to improve things — not just to generate reports that sit on a shelf. There's a lot of survey fatigue in academia, and I think people fill these out because they want to believe someone's listening. I'd like to think that's true here.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. I get to spend my days thinking hard about problems that actually matter to me, and that's not nothing. it can feel pretty disconnected from the world outside the lab sometimes — which is its own frustration — but the work itself keeps me going.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's hard for me to explain in details without specific questions/prompts, but I feel like over all, I am under the impression that the school and department don't quite care about anything but our performance (e.g. publications, awards, funding, etc.). Social events receive support from the department only when it comes hand-in-hand with speakers or posters, or some sort of academic purposes. There is a lack of support for personal developments, or even interests in non-academic careers, from the department of chemistry at my school.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The disconnection of science to the public

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: This may be different for other people, but I think many of the questions I have answered (mostly about what career opportunities are out there) can also be beneficial to undergraduate students. Coming from a small liberal art college, I don't think I know about many of the research area as I do now. Maybe because many research fields have become "hot topics" in recent years due to the advantage of social media and podcasts (that interesting findings have been better communicated), but an awareness between scientific communities and the general public doesn't hurt. Additionally, I feel like I didn't know at all what to expect from graduate programs. (My undergrad teachers showed me 'the PhD' movie and that was that). Though expectations can be hard because I think working environments are so different even from lab to lab, within a department.

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: I'm in between several industry careers (medical related - applied science, or more research based). I haven't looked closely enough into governments and non-profit positions, but I wouldn't be opposed to those. I also thought about science communication as a career.

Q26.text: Honestly, pretty broken in a lot of ways. The system rewards individual achievement over collaboration, and it creates this culture where everyone's competing rather than building something together. I came in expecting a community and found the opposite. it's exhausting and kind of demoralising to be honest.

Q16.text: Funding cuts and the complete absence of any real mentorship structure.

Q55.text: That supervisors are largely absent and you're basically on your own from day one. I think I assumed there'd be this ongoing relationship, regular guidance, someone invested in your development. Instead you figure it out alone. Knowing that upfront would've saved me a lot of disappointment.

Q41.text: Teaching, outreach, maybe some light research on the side.

Q60.text: Not really, I think I've said what I wanted to say. The isolation and lack of community is the thing that gets to me most — I hope that comes through.

Q17.text: The freedom to read widely and follow ideas wherever they go. That part I genuinely like. it's just hard to enjoy it when there's no one to share it with.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I can repeat what I wrote above. I think there is too much time alone. I had expected to become part of a creative and established research group, but there is basicaly no group. Everyone is occupied with their own businesses. There is also no proper introduction for phd-students at the department and you are left alone to figure out where to go and what to do. And that you are trained to think egoistic and not collaborative is not constructive! At least not to me.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The unhealthy egoistic culture in academia. I think high-quality research evolves from smart people working together thinking out solutions together, however, the competitiveness between researchers and the little available funding destroy this possibility. I think it is an unhealthy culture to be part of. Furthermore, publications in high-impact journals are valued more than for instance teaching experience and ability when you apply for permanent positions. I think society looses a lot on this, as we end up with a lot of (again) egoistic people at the universities, who then is forced to teach, but feel that it is a waste of time and the result is low-quality teaching.

Q55.text: That my main-advisor is not a group person but works better individually, which is completely opposite of me. That both my main supervisors always travel and very seldom are present at the department (contributing to even less research group feeling).

Q26.text: Hierarchical and often stifling, tbh. There's so much intellectual energy in academia, but the system channels it through these rigid power structures where the supervisor holds nearly all the cards. we feel the curiosity, the drive -- but it gets filtered through approval chains and gatekeeping. And I think that dampens motivation more than people here are willing to admit.

Q16.text: Honestly the thing that has concerned us most -- beyond what was already mentioned -- is how invisible the system's opportunity map is until it's too late. We only recently learned that a translational research background could open doors at places like MIT or Yale, and by then certain paths had already narrowed. that kind of institutional blindness should be addressed much earlier in the PhD.

Q55.text: That the supervisor relationship defines almost everything -- your productivity, your wellbeing, your future options. We went in thinking the research topic was the most important decision, but in hindsight the supervisor choice mattered far more. knowing that earlier would have changed how we evaluated the whole opportunity entirely.

Q60.text: Not really -- except to say that surveys like this one matter more than people realise. The PhD experience shapes researchers in ways that last decades, and if the system keeps ignoring the structural problems we've described, it will keep losing good scientists to frustration and circumstance.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, when we actually get to exercise it. There's something genuinely exciting about sitting with a hard problem and knowing your whole job is to figure it out. That part hasn't lost its appeal, even when everything around it -- the politics, the hierarchy -- makes it harder than it should be.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Research opportunities are great but we cannot do what we want. Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni

Q60.text: I think a lot of the uncertainty about phD careers arises from the vastly different experience each trainee has during graduate school. For example, one trainee may work 70 hours per week, manage a budget, run multiple projects at once, and publish 4 first-author publications as well as a handful of non-first author publications. Meanwhile, another trainee in the same department might work 30 hours per week on their own personal project, is well-read, becomes a member in multiple peer groups/societies, maintains a vibrant social life and extracurricular agenda, and overall is a more well-rounded person. While the first person is likely to move on to a competitive academic post-doc, which of these two is most competitive for the non-academic position? Would one of these trainees out perform the other in a non-academic position? How does the public perceive these two candidates? Do they recognize the merits of each, or would they solely focus on the fact that this person has a phD?
